units.title: What a company sells
units.summary: Revenue is where every analysis starts: how much a company sells and how fast that is growing.

lessons.title: Revenue: the top line
lessons.intro: **Revenue** (also called sales or the *top line*) is the total money a company brings in from customers during its fiscal year, before paying any costs. It sits on the first line of the income statement. Company reports print it in huge raw numbers, so analysts shorten them: **M** for million, **B** for billion, **T** for trillion. $416,161,000,000 becomes $416.2B. Revenue tells you the *scale* of a business, not whether it is profitable: a grocery chain can have enormous sales and thin profits. In this lesson you'll read and compare the revenue of real companies.

lessons.title: Revenue growth
lessons.intro: **Revenue growth** tells you how much bigger (or smaller) sales got compared with the year before. The formula is simple: **this year ÷ last year − 1**. If revenue went from $100B to $112B, growth is 112 ÷ 100 − 1 = 12%. Always divide by the *earlier* year; dividing by the later year understates growth. Growth can be negative, which means sales shrank. A fast grower and a slow grower can both be good businesses, but growth is one of the biggest drivers of how the market values a company.

questions.prompt: NVIDIA (NVDA)'s revenue went from $60.9B in FY2024 to $130.5B in FY2025. By what percentage did revenue grow?
questions.explanation: Revenue growth = this year's revenue ÷ last year's revenue − 1 = $130.5B ÷ $60.9B − 1 = 114.2%. Revenue grew by 114.2% in one year. Common slip: dividing the change by the new year instead of the old gives 53.3%.

lessons.title: Compounding: 3-year CAGR
lessons.intro: One year of growth can be a fluke. The **compound annual growth rate (CAGR)** smooths several years into a single per-year rate: **(end ÷ start)^(1/years) − 1**. Why not just divide total growth by the number of years? Because growth compounds: each year grows on top of the last. Revenue that rises 33% over three years grew about 10% a year, not 11%. CAGR is the fairest way to compare growth across companies and to feed a growth assumption into a valuation later in the course.

questions.prompt: Tesla (TSLA)'s revenue was $53.8B in FY2021 and $97.7B in FY2024. What was its compound annual growth rate (CAGR) over those 3 years?
questions.explanation: 3-year revenue growth rate (CAGR) = (revenue now ÷ revenue 3 years ago)^(1/3) − 1 = ($97.7B ÷ $53.8B)^(1/3) − 1 = 22.0% per year. Compounding means each year's growth builds on the last, so the per-year rate is less than total growth ÷ 3. Common slip: dividing total growth by 3 (ignores compounding) gives 27.2%.

units.title: Margins
units.summary: Margins show how many cents of each sales dollar a company keeps at each step of the income statement.

lessons.title: Gross profit & gross margin
lessons.intro: **Gross profit** is revenue minus the **cost of revenue**: what it cost to make or purchase the things the company sold. **Gross margin** is gross profit ÷ revenue. A software company with a 70% gross margin keeps 70 cents of each sales dollar after delivering its product; a warehouse retailer might keep 12 cents. Neither is automatically better. Low-margin retailers can win on volume, while high gross margins leave room to spend on research and marketing. The classic mistake is using net income instead of gross profit.

questions.prompt: In FY2024, Coca-Cola (KO) had revenue of $47.1B and cost of revenue of $18.3B. What was its gross profit?
questions.explanation: Gross profit = revenue − cost of revenue = $47.1B − $18.3B = $28.7B. Gross profit is what's left from sales after paying for the products or services themselves. Common slip: adding cost instead of subtracting it gives $65.4B.

questions.prompt: In FY2024, Procter & Gamble (PG) had revenue of $84.0B and gross profit of $43.2B. What was its gross margin?
questions.explanation: Gross margin = gross profit ÷ revenue = $43.2B ÷ $84.0B = 51.4%. Out of every $1 of sales, Procter & Gamble kept about 51 cents after paying for what it sold. Common slip: using operating income gives 22.1%.

questions.prompt: In FY2024, Johnson & Johnson (JNJ) had revenue of $88.8B and gross profit of $61.4B. What was its gross margin? Answer as a percentage (e.g. 12.5%).

questions.prompt: Which company had the higher gross margin in its latest fiscal year?

lessons.title: Operating margin
lessons.intro: Below gross profit come the costs of running the business: research and development, sales and marketing, and general administration. Subtract them and you get **operating income**, the profit from the core business before interest and taxes. **Operating margin** = operating income ÷ revenue. It shows how efficiently a company turns sales into profit from what it actually does. If the margin is negative, the business spent more to run itself than its products earned. Watch the trend across years: rising operating margins often mean a company is getting more efficient as it grows.

questions.prompt: In FY2024, Amazon.com (AMZN) had revenue of $638.0B and operating income of $68.6B. What was its operating margin?
questions.explanation: Operating margin = operating income ÷ revenue = $68.6B ÷ $638.0B = 10.8%. After product costs and running the business (R&D, sales, admin), Amazon.com kept about 11 cents per $1 of sales. Common slip: using gross profit gives 48.9%.

questions.prompt: In FY2024, Coca-Cola (KO) had revenue of $47.1B and operating income of $10.0B. What was its operating margin? Answer as a percentage (e.g. 12.5%).
questions.explanation: Operating margin = operating income ÷ revenue = $10.0B ÷ $47.1B = 21.2%. After product costs and running the business (R&D, sales, admin), Coca-Cola kept about 21 cents per $1 of sales.

lessons.title: Net margin
lessons.intro: **Net income** is what remains after *everything*: product costs, operating expenses, interest, one-off charges and taxes. **Net margin** = net income ÷ revenue, the famous "bottom line" as a share of sales. Because it includes one-time items and tax quirks, net margin can jump around more than operating margin. A company can have a healthy operating margin but a weak net margin if it carries lots of debt (interest) or takes a big write-down. Compare net margin to operating margin to spot those gaps.

lessons.title: The margin stack
lessons.intro: Put the three margins together and you get the **margin stack**: gross margin at the top, operating margin in the middle, net margin at the bottom. The gap between gross and operating margin is the share of revenue spent on **operating expenses** (R&D, sales, admin). A company with a high gross margin but a low operating margin is spending heavily, maybe investing for growth, maybe running inefficiently. Reading the stack tells you *where* the money goes, which is more useful than any single margin.

Gross margin minus operating margin is the slice of each sales dollar (15 cents) spent running the business. Common slip: reporting gross margin gives 46.9%.

units.title: Profit & EPS
units.summary: From total profit to one share's slice of it, and what taxes take along the way.

lessons.title: Net income
lessons.intro: **Net income** is the company's profit after every cost, interest payment and tax, the last line of the income statement. You can reconstruct it from revenue and net margin: **net income = revenue × net margin**. A company with huge revenue can still earn less than a smaller, more profitable rival. When net income is negative, the company reported a **net loss** for the year. Losses aren't automatically bad (young or cyclical companies have them), but they do mean the business consumed value that year instead of creating it.

questions.prompt: In FY2025, NVIDIA (NVDA) had revenue of $130.5B and a net margin of 55.8%. Roughly how much net income (profit after all costs and taxes) did it earn?
questions.explanation: Net income = revenue × net margin = $130.5B × 55.8% = $72.9B. Net income is the bottom line of the income statement: revenue minus every cost, interest and tax. Common slip: using 1 − net margin gives $57.6B.

questions.prompt: Which company had the higher net income in its latest fiscal year?
questions.explanation: Net income = revenue × net margin. Apple (AAPL), FY2025: $416.2B × 26.9% = $112.0B. Tesla (TSLA), FY2024: $97.7B × 7.3% = $7.1B. So Apple (AAPL) is higher. (Latest fiscal years differ, so the periods don't line up exactly.)

questions.prompt: True or false? Costco Wholesale (COST) reported a profit (positive net income) in FY2025.
questions.explanation: True: net income was $8.1B. A negative bottom line is called a net loss.

questions.prompt: Rank these companies from highest to lowest net income (latest fiscal year).

questions.prompt: In FY2025, Micron Technology (MU) had revenue of $37.4B and a net margin of 22.8%. Roughly how much net income (profit after all costs and taxes) did it earn? Answer in dollars (e.g. $12.3B).
questions.explanation: Net income = revenue × net margin = $37.4B × 22.8% = $8.5B. Net income is the bottom line of the income statement: revenue minus every cost, interest and tax.

questions.prompt: True or false? Exxon Mobil (XOM)'s net income in FY2024 was above $44.0B.
questions.explanation: False. Net income = revenue × net margin = $349.6B × 9.6% = $33.7B, which is below $44.0B. Net income is the bottom line of the income statement: revenue minus every cost, interest and tax.

lessons.title: Earnings per share
lessons.intro: If you own one share, your slice of the profit is **earnings per share (EPS)** = net income ÷ shares outstanding. Analysts use **diluted** shares, which count stock options and other securities that could turn into shares. EPS lets you track profit growth from a single owner's point of view: if a company repurchases shares, EPS rises even when total profit stays flat. Don't compare EPS *between* companies. A $20 EPS isn't better than $2 if the share prices are $900 and $50.

questions.prompt: In FY2025, NVIDIA (NVDA) earned net income of $72.9B with 24.80 billion diluted shares. What was its earnings per share?
questions.explanation: Earnings per share (EPS) = net income ÷ diluted shares = $72.9B ÷ 24.80B shares = $2.94. EPS is one share's slice of the year's profit. Different companies have very different share counts, so compare EPS over time, not across companies. Common slip: dividing revenue by shares gives $5.26.

lessons.title: EPS growth
lessons.intro: **EPS growth** = this year's EPS ÷ last year's EPS − 1. It's the per-share version of profit growth and the number most often quoted in earnings headlines. EPS growth can differ from net income growth because of **buybacks** (fewer shares means a bigger slice each) or **dilution** (new shares shrink each slice). Big swings are common after a bad year: going from $0.70 to $7.59 is growth of nearly 1,000%, which says more about how weak the starting year was than about the future.

questions.prompt: Exxon Mobil (XOM)'s diluted EPS went from $8.89 in FY2023 to $7.84 in FY2024. By what percentage did EPS change?
questions.explanation: EPS growth = this year's EPS ÷ last year's EPS − 1 = $7.84 ÷ $8.89 − 1 = -11.8%. EPS can grow faster than net income when a company repurchases shares, because the profit is split across fewer shares. Common slip: forgetting to subtract 1 gives 88.2%.

questions.prompt: Johnson & Johnson (JNJ)'s diluted EPS went from $13.76 in FY2023 to $5.79 in FY2024. By what percentage did EPS change? Answer as a percentage (e.g. 12.5%).
questions.explanation: EPS growth = this year's EPS ÷ last year's EPS − 1 = $5.79 ÷ $13.76 − 1 = -57.9%. EPS can grow faster than net income when a company repurchases shares, because the profit is split across fewer shares.

questions.prompt: Which company had the lower EPS growth in its latest fiscal year?
questions.explanation: EPS growth = this year's EPS ÷ last year's EPS − 1. Microsoft (MSFT), FY2025: $13.64 ÷ $11.80 − 1 = 15.6%. JPMorgan Chase (JPM), FY2024: $19.75 ÷ $16.23 − 1 = 21.7%. So Microsoft (MSFT) is lower. (Latest fiscal years differ, so the periods don't line up exactly.)

questions.prompt: True or false? Coca-Cola (KO)'s EPS growth in FY2024 was above -3.0%.
questions.explanation: True. EPS growth = this year's EPS ÷ last year's EPS − 1 = $2.46 ÷ $2.47 − 1 = -0.4%, which is above -3.0%. EPS can grow faster than net income when a company repurchases shares, because the profit is split across fewer shares.

questions.explanation: EPS growth = this year's EPS ÷ last year's EPS − 1. Highest to lowest: Amazon.com (AMZN) 90.7%; JPMorgan Chase (JPM) 21.7%; Coca-Cola (KO) -0.4%; Tesla (TSLA) -52.6%.

questions.prompt: Micron Technology (MU)'s diluted EPS went from $0.70 in FY2024 to $7.59 in FY2025. By what percentage did EPS change?
questions.explanation: EPS growth = this year's EPS ÷ last year's EPS − 1 = $7.59 ÷ $0.70 − 1 = 984.3%. EPS can grow faster than net income when a company repurchases shares, because the profit is split across fewer shares. Common slip: dividing the change by the new year gives 90.8%.

lessons.title: Taxes: the effective rate
lessons.intro: Governments take a cut of profits. The **effective tax rate** = income tax ÷ pre-tax income. It's what the company actually paid, and it often differs from the 21% US federal rate because of foreign profits, tax credits, and one-time items. A sudden drop in the tax rate can make net income jump without the business improving at all. That's why analysts also look at operating income, which comes before tax. Only calculate the rate when pre-tax income is positive; with a loss the ratio is meaningless.

questions.prompt: In FY2025, Micron Technology (MU) had pre-tax income of $9.7B and paid income tax of $1.1B. What was its effective tax rate?
questions.explanation: Effective tax rate = income tax ÷ pre-tax income = $1.1B ÷ $9.7B = 11.6%. The effective rate is what the company actually paid; it differs from the 21% US headline rate because of foreign profits, credits and one-offs. Common slip: dividing tax by revenue gives 3.0%.

questions.prompt: In FY2024, Exxon Mobil (XOM) had pre-tax income of $47.4B and paid income tax of $13.8B. What was its effective tax rate? Answer as a percentage (e.g. 12.5%).

units.title: Cash flow & FCF
units.summary: Profit is an opinion, cash is a fact: reading the cash-flow statement.

lessons.title: Cash from operations vs. profit
lessons.intro: Net income follows accounting rules, which count some costs that aren't paid in cash (like **depreciation**, the slow write-off of equipment) and some sales that haven't been collected yet. The cash-flow statement fixes that. **Operating cash flow (OCF)** is the cash the business actually generated from its operations. Comparing OCF with net income, a ratio we'll call **cash conversion**, is a quick quality check. Consistently above 1x is a healthy sign; profits that never turn into cash deserve a closer look.

questions.prompt: In FY2024, Procter & Gamble (PG) reported net income of $14.9B and operating cash flow of $19.8B. What was its cash conversion (operating cash flow ÷ net income)?
questions.explanation: Cash conversion = operating cash flow ÷ net income = $19.8B ÷ $14.9B = 1.33x. Above 1x means the business brought in more cash than its reported profit (often thanks to non-cash costs like depreciation). Common slip: dividing the wrong way round gives 0.75x.

questions.prompt: In FY2024, Exxon Mobil (XOM) reported net income of $33.7B and operating cash flow of $55.0B. What was its cash conversion (operating cash flow ÷ net income)? Answer as a multiple (e.g. 18.2x).
questions.explanation: Cash conversion = operating cash flow ÷ net income = $55.0B ÷ $33.7B = 1.63x. Above 1x means the business brought in more cash than its reported profit (often thanks to non-cash costs like depreciation).

questions.prompt: True or false? Tesla (TSLA)'s operating cash flow was larger than its net income in FY2024.
questions.explanation: True: operating cash flow $14.9B vs. net income $7.1B. Net income follows accounting rules; operating cash flow counts the cash that actually came in.

questions.prompt: Which company had the higher cash conversion in its latest fiscal year?
questions.explanation: Cash conversion = operating cash flow ÷ net income. NVIDIA (NVDA), FY2025: $64.1B ÷ $72.9B = 0.88x. Micron Technology (MU), FY2025: $17.5B ÷ $8.5B = 2.05x. So Micron Technology (MU) is higher.

questions.prompt: Rank these companies from highest to lowest cash conversion (latest fiscal year).
questions.explanation: Cash conversion = operating cash flow ÷ net income. Highest to lowest: Amazon.com (AMZN) 1.96x; Exxon Mobil (XOM) 1.63x; Procter & Gamble (PG) 1.33x; NVIDIA (NVDA) 0.88x. (Latest fiscal years differ, so the periods don't line up exactly.)

questions.prompt: True or false? Microsoft (MSFT)'s operating cash flow was larger than its net income in FY2025.
questions.explanation: True: operating cash flow $136.2B vs. net income $101.8B. Net income follows accounting rules; operating cash flow counts the cash that actually came in.

questions.prompt: In FY2024, Johnson & Johnson (JNJ) reported net income of $14.1B and operating cash flow of $24.3B. What was its cash conversion (operating cash flow ÷ net income)?
questions.explanation: Cash conversion = operating cash flow ÷ net income = $24.3B ÷ $14.1B = 1.73x. Above 1x means the business brought in more cash than its reported profit (often thanks to non-cash costs like depreciation). Common slip: dividing the wrong way round gives 0.58x.

lessons.title: Free cash flow
lessons.intro: Operating cash flow isn't all spare cash: a company must also spend on **capital expenditures (capex)**, which means factories, equipment, data centers and stores. **Free cash flow (FCF) = operating cash flow − capex**. It's the cash left over that could pay dividends, repurchase shares, repay debt or pile up in the bank. The most common slip is adding capex instead of subtracting it. FCF can be negative in heavy investment years even for a healthy company. What matters is whether the spending eventually pays off.

questions.prompt: In FY2025, Costco Wholesale (COST) generated $13.3B of operating cash flow and spent $5.5B on capital expenditures. What was its free cash flow?
questions.explanation: Free cash flow = operating cash flow − capital expenditures = $13.3B − $5.5B = $7.8B. Free cash flow is the cash left after keeping the business running and growing; it can fund dividends, buybacks, debt paydown or savings. Common slip: adding capex instead of subtracting it gives $18.8B.

questions.prompt: In FY2025, Micron Technology (MU) generated $17.5B of operating cash flow and spent $15.9B on capital expenditures. What was its free cash flow? Answer in dollars (e.g. $12.3B).
questions.explanation: Free cash flow = operating cash flow − capital expenditures = $17.5B − $15.9B = $1.7B. Free cash flow is the cash left after keeping the business running and growing; it can fund dividends, buybacks, debt paydown or savings.

questions.prompt: True or false? Tesla (TSLA)'s free cash flow in FY2024 was above $2.5B.
questions.explanation: True. Free cash flow = operating cash flow − capital expenditures = $14.9B − $11.3B = $3.6B, which is above $2.5B. Free cash flow is the cash left after keeping the business running and growing; it can fund dividends, buybacks, debt paydown or savings.

questions.prompt: Which company had the higher free cash flow in its latest fiscal year?
questions.explanation: Free cash flow = operating cash flow − capital expenditures. NVIDIA (NVDA), FY2025: $64.1B − $3.2B = $60.9B. Coca-Cola (KO), FY2024: $6.8B − $2.1B = $4.7B. So NVIDIA (NVDA) is higher. (Latest fiscal years differ, so the periods don't line up exactly.)

questions.explanation: Free cash flow = operating cash flow − capital expenditures. Highest to lowest: Microsoft (MSFT) $71.6B; NVIDIA (NVDA) $60.9B; Coca-Cola (KO) $4.7B; Tesla (TSLA) $3.6B. (Latest fiscal years differ, so the periods don't line up exactly.)

questions.prompt: In FY2024, Procter & Gamble (PG) generated $19.8B of operating cash flow and spent $3.3B on capital expenditures. What was its free cash flow?
questions.explanation: Free cash flow = operating cash flow − capital expenditures = $19.8B − $3.3B = $16.5B. Free cash flow is the cash left after keeping the business running and growing; it can fund dividends, buybacks, debt paydown or savings. Common slip: adding capex instead of subtracting it gives $23.2B.

lessons.title: FCF margin
lessons.intro: Just like profit margins, you can express free cash flow as a share of revenue: **FCF margin = free cash flow ÷ revenue**. It tells you how many cents of each sales dollar end up as spare cash after the company has paid to run *and* reinvest in the business. Asset-light software companies often have FCF margins above 30%, while retailers and manufacturers are usually in single digits. Comparing FCF margin with net margin shows whether reported profits are backed by cash.

questions.prompt: In FY2025, NVIDIA (NVDA) had revenue of $130.5B, operating cash flow of $64.1B and capex of $3.2B. What was its free-cash-flow margin?
questions.explanation: FCF margin = free cash flow ÷ revenue = ($64.1B − $3.2B) ÷ $130.5B = $60.9B ÷ $130.5B = 46.6%. Each $1 of sales turned into about 47 cents of free cash. Common slip: using net income gives 55.8%.

questions.prompt: In FY2025, Apple (AAPL) had revenue of $416.2B, operating cash flow of $111.5B and capex of $12.7B. What was its free-cash-flow margin? Answer as a percentage (e.g. 12.5%).
questions.explanation: FCF margin = free cash flow ÷ revenue = ($111.5B − $12.7B) ÷ $416.2B = $98.8B ÷ $416.2B = 23.7%. Each $1 of sales turned into about 24 cents of free cash.

questions.prompt: Which company had the higher FCF margin in its latest fiscal year?
questions.explanation: FCF margin = free cash flow ÷ revenue. Exxon Mobil (XOM), FY2024: ($55.0B − $24.3B) ÷ $349.6B = $30.7B ÷ $349.6B = 8.8%. Micron Technology (MU), FY2025: ($17.5B − $15.9B) ÷ $37.4B = $1.7B ÷ $37.4B = 4.5%. So Exxon Mobil (XOM) is higher. (Latest fiscal years differ, so the periods don't line up exactly.)

questions.prompt: True or false? Johnson & Johnson (JNJ)'s FCF margin in FY2024 was above 16.0%.
questions.explanation: True. FCF margin = free cash flow ÷ revenue = ($24.3B − $4.4B) ÷ $88.8B = $19.8B ÷ $88.8B = 22.3%, which is above 16.0%. Each $1 of sales turned into about 22 cents of free cash.

questions.prompt: Rank these companies from highest to lowest FCF margin (latest fiscal year).
questions.explanation: FCF margin = free cash flow ÷ revenue. Highest to lowest: NVIDIA (NVDA) 46.6%; Procter & Gamble (PG) 19.7%; Coca-Cola (KO) 10.1%; Micron Technology (MU) 4.5%. (Latest fiscal years differ, so the periods don't line up exactly.)

questions.prompt: In FY2024, Tesla (TSLA) had revenue of $97.7B, operating cash flow of $14.9B and capex of $11.3B. What was its free-cash-flow margin?
questions.explanation: FCF margin = free cash flow ÷ revenue = ($14.9B − $11.3B) ÷ $97.7B = $3.6B ÷ $97.7B = 3.7%. Each $1 of sales turned into about 3.7 cents of free cash. Common slip: forgetting to subtract capex gives 15.3%.

lessons.title: Capex intensity
lessons.intro: Some businesses need huge, constant investment just to stay competitive. **Capex intensity = capex ÷ revenue** measures how much of each sales dollar goes back into physical assets. Chipmakers building fabs can spend 30-45% of revenue on capex; a software company might spend under 5%, and much of that on data centers. High capex intensity isn't bad, but it means less free cash flow per dollar of profit, and the return on all that spending really matters. You'll measure that return in the next unit.

questions.prompt: In FY2024, Johnson & Johnson (JNJ) had revenue of $88.8B and capital expenditures of $4.4B. What was its capex intensity (capex ÷ revenue)?
questions.explanation: Capex intensity = capital expenditures ÷ revenue = $4.4B ÷ $88.8B = 5.0%. Johnson & Johnson reinvested about 5.0 cents of every sales dollar in factories, equipment, data centers or stores. Common slip: dividing capex by operating cash flow gives 18.2%.

questions.prompt: In FY2024, Procter & Gamble (PG) had revenue of $84.0B and capital expenditures of $3.3B. What was its capex intensity (capex ÷ revenue)? Answer as a percentage (e.g. 12.5%).
questions.explanation: Capex intensity = capital expenditures ÷ revenue = $3.3B ÷ $84.0B = 4.0%. Procter & Gamble reinvested about 4.0 cents of every sales dollar in factories, equipment, data centers or stores.

questions.prompt: Which company had the higher capex intensity in its latest fiscal year?
questions.explanation: Capex intensity = capital expenditures ÷ revenue. Micron Technology (MU), FY2025: $15.9B ÷ $37.4B = 42.4%. Tesla (TSLA), FY2024: $11.3B ÷ $97.7B = 11.6%. So Micron Technology (MU) is higher. (Latest fiscal years differ, so the periods don't line up exactly.)

questions.explanation: Capex intensity = capital expenditures ÷ revenue. Highest to lowest: Amazon.com (AMZN) 13.0%; Exxon Mobil (XOM) 7.0%; Coca-Cola (KO) 4.4%; Costco Wholesale (COST) 2.0%. (Latest fiscal years differ, so the periods don't line up exactly.)

units.title: Balance sheet & debt
units.summary: What a company owns, what it owes, and whether it can pay its bills.

lessons.title: Assets = liabilities + equity
lessons.intro: The balance sheet is a snapshot on the last day of the fiscal year. **Assets** are what the company owns (cash, inventory, factories, patents). **Liabilities** are what it owes (debt, unpaid bills, taxes due). The difference is **shareholders' equity**: the owners' claim on what's left. It always balances: **assets = liabilities + equity**, so equity = assets − liabilities. Equity is an accounting number, not a market price, and buybacks can shrink it a lot even at very profitable companies.

questions.prompt: At the end of FY2024, Johnson & Johnson (JNJ) had total assets of $180.1B and total liabilities of $108.6B. How much shareholders' equity did it have?
questions.explanation: Shareholders' equity = total assets − total liabilities = $180.1B − $108.6B = $71.5B. Assets = liabilities + equity always balances; equity is the owners' claim on what's left after all obligations. Common slip: adding liabilities to assets gives $288.7B.

questions.prompt: At the end of FY2024, Procter & Gamble (PG) had total assets of $122.4B and total liabilities of $71.8B. How much shareholders' equity did it have? Answer in dollars (e.g. $12.3B).
questions.explanation: Shareholders' equity = total assets − total liabilities = $122.4B − $71.8B = $50.6B. Assets = liabilities + equity always balances; equity is the owners' claim on what's left after all obligations.

questions.prompt: True or false? NVIDIA (NVDA)'s shareholders' equity in FY2025 was above $56.0B.
questions.explanation: True. Shareholders' equity = total assets − total liabilities = $111.6B − $32.3B = $79.3B, which is above $56.0B. Assets = liabilities + equity always balances; equity is the owners' claim on what's left after all obligations.

questions.prompt: Which company had the lower shareholders' equity in its latest fiscal year?
questions.explanation: Shareholders' equity = total assets − total liabilities. Microsoft (MSFT), FY2025: $619.0B − $275.5B = $343.5B. Coca-Cola (KO), FY2024: $100.5B − $75.1B = $25.5B. So Coca-Cola (KO) is lower. (Latest fiscal years differ, so the periods don't line up exactly.)

questions.prompt: Rank these companies from highest to lowest shareholders' equity (latest fiscal year).
questions.explanation: Shareholders' equity = total assets − total liabilities. Highest to lowest: Microsoft (MSFT) $343.5B; Exxon Mobil (XOM) $270.6B; Johnson & Johnson (JNJ) $71.5B; Costco Wholesale (COST) $29.2B. (Latest fiscal years differ, so the periods don't line up exactly.)

questions.prompt: At the end of FY2025, Apple (AAPL) had total assets of $359.2B and total liabilities of $285.5B. How much shareholders' equity did it have?
questions.explanation: Shareholders' equity = total assets − total liabilities = $359.2B − $285.5B = $73.7B. Assets = liabilities + equity always balances; equity is the owners' claim on what's left after all obligations. Common slip: adding liabilities to assets gives $644.7B.

lessons.title: Net cash vs. net debt
lessons.intro: Debt matters less if a company holds a pile of cash to match it. **Net cash = cash − total debt**. If the result is positive, the company could repay every lender tomorrow and still have money left. If it's negative, the company has **net debt**. Net debt isn't automatically dangerous: steady businesses often borrow at low rates on purpose. But in a downturn, net cash gives a company time while net debt demands interest payments no matter what. You'll use net cash again when you value a company.

questions.prompt: At the end of FY2024, Tesla (TSLA) held $16.1B of cash and investments and had $8.1B of total debt. What was its net cash (negative means net debt)?
questions.explanation: Net cash = cash − total debt = $16.1B − $8.1B = $8.0B. Tesla could repay all its debt from cash and still have $8.0B left. Common slip: adding debt to cash gives $24.2B.

questions.prompt: At the end of FY2025, Costco Wholesale (COST) held $14.2B of cash and investments and had $5.7B of total debt. What was its net cash (negative means net debt)? Answer in dollars (e.g. $12.3B).
questions.explanation: Net cash = cash − total debt = $14.2B − $5.7B = $8.4B. Costco Wholesale could repay all its debt from cash and still have $8.4B left.

questions.prompt: True or false? At the end of FY2025, Microsoft (MSFT) held more cash than debt.
questions.explanation: False: cash $30.2B vs. debt $43.2B. A company with more cash than debt is in a 'net cash' position; the opposite is 'net debt'.

questions.prompt: Which company had the lower net cash in its latest fiscal year?
questions.explanation: Net cash = cash − total debt. Amazon.com (AMZN), FY2024: $78.8B − $57.7B = $21.1B. Procter & Gamble (PG), FY2024: $9.5B − $32.5B = -$23.0B. So Procter & Gamble (PG) is lower.

questions.prompt: Rank these companies from highest to lowest net cash (latest fiscal year).

questions.prompt: True or false? At the end of FY2025, Micron Technology (MU) held more cash than debt.
questions.explanation: False: cash $9.6B vs. debt $15.4B. A company with more cash than debt is in a 'net cash' position; the opposite is 'net debt'.

questions.prompt: At the end of FY2025, NVIDIA (NVDA) held $8.6B of cash and investments and had $8.5B of total debt. What was its net cash (negative means net debt)?
questions.explanation: Net cash = cash − total debt = $8.6B − $8.5B = $126.0M. NVIDIA could repay all its debt from cash and still have $126.0M left. Common slip: adding debt to cash gives $17.1B.

lessons.title: Debt-to-equity
lessons.intro: **Debt-to-equity (D/E) = total debt ÷ shareholders' equity**. It shows how much the company leans on borrowed money compared with the owners' capital. A D/E of 0.2x is conservative; 2x or more is heavy leverage, which magnifies both good and bad years. Be careful: companies that repurchase lots of stock shrink their equity, which can push D/E very high even when the debt is easily covered by cash flow. Always read D/E alongside net cash and cash flow.

questions.prompt: At the end of FY2025, Micron Technology (MU) had total debt of $15.4B and shareholders' equity of $54.2B. What was its debt-to-equity ratio?
questions.explanation: Debt-to-equity = total debt ÷ shareholders' equity = $15.4B ÷ $54.2B = 0.28x. For every $1 of equity, Micron Technology carried about $0.28 of debt. Buybacks can shrink equity and push this ratio up even when debt is steady. Common slip: dividing the wrong way round gives 3.53x.

questions.prompt: At the end of FY2024, Procter & Gamble (PG) had total debt of $32.5B and shareholders' equity of $50.6B. What was its debt-to-equity ratio? Answer as a multiple (e.g. 18.2x).
questions.explanation: Debt-to-equity = total debt ÷ shareholders' equity = $32.5B ÷ $50.6B = 0.64x. For every $1 of equity, Procter & Gamble carried about $0.64 of debt. Buybacks can shrink equity and push this ratio up even when debt is steady.

questions.prompt: Which company had the higher debt-to-equity in its latest fiscal year?

questions.prompt: At the end of FY2024, Johnson & Johnson (JNJ) had total debt of $36.6B and shareholders' equity of $71.5B. What was its debt-to-equity ratio?

Buybacks can shrink equity and push this ratio up even when debt is steady. Common slip: dividing the wrong way round gives 1.95x.

lessons.title: Current ratio
lessons.intro: **Current** on a balance sheet means "within about a year." **Current assets** (cash, receivables, inventory) can be turned into cash soon; **current liabilities** (supplier bills, short-term debt) are due soon. **Current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities**. Above 1x, short-term resources cover short-term obligations. Below 1x isn't always a warning sign: big retailers collect cash from shoppers before they pay suppliers, so they run below 1x on purpose. Context matters more than any rule of thumb.

questions.prompt: At the end of FY2025, Micron Technology (MU) had current assets of $28.8B and current liabilities of $11.5B. What was its current ratio?

units.title: Returns on capital
units.summary: How much profit a business squeezes out of the money invested in it.

lessons.title: Return on equity (ROE)
lessons.intro: **Return on equity (ROE) = net income ÷ shareholders' equity**. It answers the question: for every dollar the owners have in the business (on the books), how much profit did it make this year? Consistently high ROE often signals a strong business. But ROE has a trap: because equity is in the denominator, anything that shrinks equity (debt-funded buybacks, large losses in past years) can inflate ROE without the business getting better. That's why we'll also look at ROA and ROIC.

lessons.title: Return on assets (ROA)
lessons.intro: **Return on assets (ROA) = net income ÷ total assets**. Instead of just the owners' money, it measures profit against *everything* the company controls, however it was financed. Banks and asset-heavy businesses usually have low ROAs (1-5%), while asset-light companies can reach 20% or more. Because ROA doesn't depend on how much debt a company uses, comparing ROA and ROE tells you how much of the ROE comes from the business itself and how much comes from leverage.

questions.prompt: In FY2025, Micron Technology (MU) earned net income of $8.5B on total assets of $82.8B. What was its return on assets?
questions.explanation: Return on assets (ROA) = net income ÷ total assets = $8.5B ÷ $82.8B = 10.3%. ROA ignores how the assets were financed, so it isn't boosted by debt the way ROE can be. Common slip: dividing by equity (that's ROE) gives 15.8%.

questions.prompt: In FY2024, Exxon Mobil (XOM) earned net income of $33.7B on total assets of $453.5B. What was its return on assets? Answer as a percentage (e.g. 12.5%).

lessons.title: Return on invested capital (ROIC)
lessons.intro: **ROIC** is many analysts' favorite quality measure. **Invested capital = debt + equity − cash**: the money lenders and owners have actually put to work. **ROIC = operating income × (1 − tax rate) ÷ invested capital**. Using after-tax operating income ignores how the company is financed, so ROIC compares businesses fairly. A company that earns a high ROIC and can keep reinvesting at that rate compounds value quickly. A company whose ROIC is below its cost of capital destroys value as it grows.

questions.prompt: At the end of FY2025, Microsoft (MSFT) had total debt of $43.2B, shareholders' equity of $343.5B and cash of $30.2B. How much invested capital did it have (debt + equity − cash)?

ROIC asks how much after-tax operating profit each $1 of capital in the business produces, whether that capital came from lenders or owners.

lessons.title: Leverage and ROE
lessons.intro: Here's the link between the returns: **ROE = ROA × equity multiplier**, where the **equity multiplier = total assets ÷ equity**. A multiplier of 5x means only one-fifth of the assets are funded by the owners; the rest is debt and other liabilities. Leverage lifts ROE in good years and deepens the damage in bad ones. When ROE is far above ROIC, check the balance sheet: the gap is usually debt or buybacks, not a better business.

units.summary: Bringing in the share price: what the market is paying for each dollar of sales, profit and cash.

lessons.title: Market cap & enterprise value
lessons.intro: Now we bring in the share price. **Market capitalization = share price × diluted shares**: what the stock market values all the shares at together. But owning a whole company also means taking on its debt and getting its cash. **Enterprise value (EV) = market cap + debt − cash** is the price of the whole business. Two companies with the same market cap can have very different EVs. (Share prices in this app are sample snapshots for teaching, and valuations move every day.)

lessons.title: P/E & earnings yield
lessons.intro: The **price-to-earnings ratio (P/E) = share price ÷ EPS**. A P/E of 25x means the market pays $25 for each $1 of last year's earnings. Flip it over and you get the **earnings yield** (EPS ÷ price): a P/E of 25x is a 4% earnings yield, which you can line up against a bond or savings rate. A P/E can't be calculated when earnings are negative. A high P/E usually means the market expects strong growth, and a low one can mean doubts about the future. It's a starting question, not a verdict.

lessons.title: P/S & EV/EBITDA

lessons.title: FCF yield & dividend yield
lessons.intro: Yields turn multiples upside down so you can compare them with interest rates. **FCF yield = free cash flow ÷ market cap** is the spare cash the business produced per dollar of market value. **Dividend yield = dividends paid ÷ market cap** is the part of that cash actually handed to shareholders. A company can have a low dividend yield but a high FCF yield if it prefers buybacks or reinvestment. A dividend that is larger than free cash flow has to be funded some other way, usually by borrowing.

lessons.title: What a P/E implies about growth
lessons.intro: Every multiple hides an assumption. A handy rough identity: **required return ≈ earnings yield + growth**. If investors want about 9% a year and a stock's earnings yield is 3% (a P/E of about 33x), the price only makes sense if earnings grow roughly **6% a year, for a very long time**. So **implied growth ≈ 9% − 1/P/E**. This reverse-engineering doesn't forecast anything. It shows what the current price already assumes, so you can ask whether that assumption looks reasonable next to the company's history.

questions.prompt: Apple (AAPL) traded at a P/E of 34.2x. Assume investors want a 9% yearly return and use: return ≈ earnings yield + growth. What long-run growth rate does that P/E imply?
questions.explanation: Growth implied by the P/E = required return − earnings yield = 9.0% − (1 ÷ 34.2x) = 9.0% − 2.9% = 6.1%. A higher P/E means a lower earnings yield, so more of the return has to come from growth. This is a rough identity for building intuition, not a forecast. Common slip: reporting the earnings yield itself gives 2.9%.

questions.prompt: Coca-Cola (KO) traded at a P/E of 27.0x. Assume investors want a 9% yearly return and use: return ≈ earnings yield + growth. What long-run growth rate does that P/E imply? Answer as a percentage (e.g. 12.5%).
questions.explanation: Growth implied by the P/E = required return − earnings yield = 9.0% − (1 ÷ 27.0x) = 9.0% − 3.7% = 5.3%. A higher P/E means a lower earnings yield, so more of the return has to come from growth. This is a rough identity for building intuition, not a forecast.

units.title: Intrinsic value
units.summary: Discounted cash flow basics: estimating what a business is worth, and why the estimate is fragile.

lessons.title: A one-line DCF
lessons.intro: A business is worth the cash it will produce in the future, **discounted** back to today, because a dollar next year is worth less than a dollar now. The simplest version assumes free cash flow grows at a steady rate *g* forever and discounts it at a rate *r*: **value = FCF × (1 + g) ÷ (r − g)**. Add net cash (or subtract net debt) to get the value of the equity, then divide by shares for a per-share figure. We'll use r = 9% and g = 2.5% throughout. These are assumptions, not facts.

questions.prompt: Microsoft (MSFT) produced $71.6B of free cash flow in FY2025 and had net cash of -$12.9B. Assume FCF grows 2.5% a year forever and a 9% discount rate. What is the one-line DCF value of the equity?
questions.explanation: One-line DCF value of the equity = FCF × (1 + g) ÷ (r − g) + net cash = $71.6B × 1.025 ÷ (9.0% − 2.5%) + (-$12.9B) = $1.12T. This growing-perpetuity formula is the simplest DCF. Every input is an assumption, so treat the output as a range, not a fact. Common slip: dividing by r instead of r − g gives $782.8B.

questions.prompt: Tesla (TSLA) produced $3.6B of free cash flow in FY2024 and had net cash of $8.0B. Assume FCF grows 2.5% a year forever and a 9% discount rate. What is the one-line DCF value of the equity? Answer in dollars (e.g. $12.3B).
questions.explanation: One-line DCF value of the equity = FCF × (1 + g) ÷ (r − g) + net cash = $3.6B × 1.025 ÷ (9.0% − 2.5%) + $8.0B = $64.6B. This growing-perpetuity formula is the simplest DCF. Every input is an assumption, so treat the output as a range, not a fact.

questions.prompt: NVIDIA (NVDA): FY2025 free cash flow $60.9B, net cash $126.0M, 24.80 billion diluted shares. Assume 2.5% growth forever and a 9% discount rate. What is the one-line DCF value per share?
questions.explanation: One-line DCF value per share = (FCF × (1 + g) ÷ (r − g) + net cash) ÷ diluted shares = ($60.9B × 1.025 ÷ (9.0% − 2.5%) + $126.0M) ÷ 24.80B shares = $959.7B ÷ 24.80B = $38.69. Dividing the equity value by the share count turns it into a per-share estimate you can line up against the share price. Common slip: dividing by r instead of r − g gives $27.26.

questions.prompt: Johnson & Johnson (JNJ): FY2024 free cash flow $19.8B, net cash -$12.5B, 2.43 billion diluted shares. Assume 2.5% growth forever and a 9% discount rate. What is the one-line DCF value per share? Answer in dollars per share (e.g. $4.20).
questions.explanation: One-line DCF value per share = (FCF × (1 + g) ÷ (r − g) + net cash) ÷ diluted shares = ($19.8B × 1.025 ÷ (9.0% − 2.5%) + (-$12.5B)) ÷ 2.43B shares = $300.4B ÷ 2.43B = $123.66. Dividing the equity value by the share count turns it into a per-share estimate you can line up against the share price.

questions.prompt: True or false? Costco Wholesale (COST)'s one-line DCF value per share in FY2025 was above $210.00.
questions.explanation: True. One-line DCF value per share = (FCF × (1 + g) ÷ (r − g) + net cash) ÷ diluted shares = ($7.8B × 1.025 ÷ (9.0% − 2.5%) + $8.4B) ÷ 0.45B shares = $132.0B ÷ 0.45B = $296.70, which is above $210.00. Dividing the equity value by the share count turns it into a per-share estimate you can line up against the share price.

questions.prompt: Apple (AAPL): FY2025 free cash flow $98.8B, net cash -$62.7B, 15.01 billion diluted shares. Assume 2.5% growth forever and a 9% discount rate. What is the one-line DCF value per share?
questions.explanation: One-line DCF value per share = (FCF × (1 + g) ÷ (r − g) + net cash) ÷ diluted shares = ($98.8B × 1.025 ÷ (9.0% − 2.5%) + (-$62.7B)) ÷ 15.01B shares = $1.49T ÷ 15.01B = $99.62. Dividing the equity value by the share count turns it into a per-share estimate you can line up against the share price. Common slip: dividing by r instead of r − g gives $68.96.

lessons.title: A two-stage DCF
lessons.intro: Most companies don't grow at 2.5% from day one. A **two-stage DCF** lets FCF grow faster for a few years (here: five years at the company's own 3-year revenue CAGR, capped at 15%), then settles into 2.5% forever. You discount each of the five years separately, then add a **terminal value** (the one-line formula applied in year 5) discounted back five years. Notice how much of the total sits in that terminal value: long-run assumptions dominate every DCF.

questions.prompt: Microsoft (MSFT): FY2025 FCF $71.6B, net cash -$12.9B, 7.46B shares. Assume FCF grows 12% a year for 5 years (its recent revenue CAGR, rounded and capped at 15%), then 2.5% forever, discounted at 9%. What is the two-stage DCF value per share?
questions.explanation: Two-stage DCF value per share = PV of 5 growth years + PV of terminal value + net cash, per share = 5 years of FCF growing 12% from $71.6B, discounted at 9%, is worth $388.7B today; the year-5 terminal value $1.99T discounted back is $1.29T; ($388.7B + $1.29T + (-$12.9B) net cash) ÷ 7.46B shares = $223.61. Most of a DCF's value usually sits in the terminal value, which is why small changes in long-run assumptions move the answer so much. Common slip: using only the one-line perpetuity gives $149.54.

questions.prompt: Procter & Gamble (PG): FY2024 FCF $16.5B, net cash -$23.0B, 2.47B shares. Assume FCF grows 3% a year for 5 years (its recent revenue CAGR, rounded and capped at 15%), then 2.5% forever, discounted at 9%. What is the two-stage DCF value per share? Answer in dollars per share (e.g. $4.20).
questions.explanation: Two-stage DCF value per share = PV of 5 growth years + PV of terminal value + net cash, per share = 5 years of FCF growing 3% from $16.5B, discounted at 9%, is worth $69.9B today; the year-5 terminal value $302.1B discounted back is $196.3B; ($69.9B + $196.3B + (-$23.0B) net cash) ÷ 2.47B shares = $98.38. Most of a DCF's value usually sits in the terminal value, which is why small changes in long-run assumptions move the answer so much.

questions.prompt: True or false? Tesla (TSLA)'s two-stage DCF value per share in FY2024 was above $21.00.
questions.explanation: True. Two-stage DCF value per share = PV of 5 growth years + PV of terminal value + net cash, per share = 5 years of FCF growing 15% from $3.6B, discounted at 9%, is worth $21.1B today; the year-5 terminal value $113.7B discounted back is $73.9B; ($21.1B + $73.9B + $8.0B net cash) ÷ 3.50B shares = $29.45, which is above $21.00. Most of a DCF's value usually sits in the terminal value, which is why small changes in long-run assumptions move the answer so much.

questions.prompt: NVIDIA (NVDA): FY2025 FCF $60.9B, net cash $126.0M, 24.80B shares. Assume FCF grows 15% a year for 5 years (its recent revenue CAGR, rounded and capped at 15%), then 2.5% forever, discounted at 9%. What is the two-stage DCF value per share?
questions.explanation: Two-stage DCF value per share = PV of 5 growth years + PV of terminal value + net cash, per share = 5 years of FCF growing 15% from $60.9B, discounted at 9%, is worth $358.4B today; the year-5 terminal value $1.93T discounted back is $1.25T; ($358.4B + $1.25T + $126.0M net cash) ÷ 24.80B shares = $65.03. Most of a DCF's value usually sits in the terminal value, which is why small changes in long-run assumptions move the answer so much. Common slip: using only the one-line perpetuity gives $38.69.

questions.prompt: Amazon.com (AMZN): FY2024 FCF $32.9B, net cash $21.1B, 10.72B shares. Assume FCF grows 11% a year for 5 years (its recent revenue CAGR, rounded and capped at 15%), then 2.5% forever, discounted at 9%. What is the two-stage DCF value per share? Answer in dollars per share (e.g. $4.20).
questions.explanation: Two-stage DCF value per share = PV of 5 growth years + PV of terminal value + net cash, per share = 5 years of FCF growing 11% from $32.9B, discounted at 9%, is worth $173.6B today; the year-5 terminal value $873.5B discounted back is $567.7B; ($173.6B + $567.7B + $21.1B net cash) ÷ 10.72B shares = $71.12. Most of a DCF's value usually sits in the terminal value, which is why small changes in long-run assumptions move the answer so much.

lessons.title: Price vs. estimate & sensitivity
lessons.intro: Once you have an estimate of value, you can compare it with the share price: **price ÷ estimate − 1**. Investors call a gap between value and price a **margin of safety**, a cushion for being wrong. But be humble about the estimate. Changing the discount rate from 10% to 8% can raise a one-line DCF by 40% or more, because *r − g* is a small number. A big gap between price and model usually means the market assumes something different from your model, so question the assumptions before trusting the answer.

questions.prompt: Procter & Gamble (PG)'s sample share price was $154.00, and a one-line DCF (9% discount rate, 2.5% growth) gave $96.07 per share. By what percentage is the price above (+) or below (−) that estimate?
questions.explanation: Gap between price and the one-line DCF = share price ÷ DCF value per share − 1 = $154.00 ÷ $96.07 − 1 = 60.3%. The gap between an estimate of value and the price is what investors call the margin of safety. A large gap often means the market is assuming very different growth than the model, so question the assumptions first. Prices are a sample snapshot for teaching; valuations move every day. Common slip: dividing the wrong way round gives -37.6%.

questions.prompt: Coca-Cola (KO)'s sample share price was $66.50, and a one-line DCF (9% discount rate, 2.5% growth) gave $8.70 per share. By what percentage is the price above (+) or below (−) that estimate? Answer as a percentage (e.g. 12.5%).
questions.explanation: Gap between price and the one-line DCF = share price ÷ DCF value per share − 1 = $66.50 ÷ $8.70 − 1 = 664.8%. The gap between an estimate of value and the price is what investors call the margin of safety. A large gap often means the market is assuming very different growth than the model, so question the assumptions first. Prices are a sample snapshot for teaching; valuations move every day.

questions.prompt: A one-line DCF of NVIDIA (NVDA) (FCF $60.9B, 2.5% growth) gives $45.73 per share at an 8% discount rate and $33.53 at 10%. How many times larger is the 8% value than the 10% value? Answer as a multiple (e.g. 18.2x).
questions.explanation: DCF sensitivity to the discount rate = value at an 8% discount rate ÷ value at a 10% discount rate = $45.73 (at 8%) ÷ $33.53 (at 10%) = 1.36x. Moving the discount rate by just 2 points changes the estimate a lot, because r − g in the denominator is a small number.

questions.prompt: A one-line DCF of Tesla (TSLA) (FCF $3.6B, 2.5% growth) gives $21.39 per share at an 8% discount rate and $16.30 at 10%. How many times larger is the 8% value than the 10% value?
questions.explanation: DCF sensitivity to the discount rate = value at an 8% discount rate ÷ value at a 10% discount rate = $21.39 (at 8%) ÷ $16.30 (at 10%) = 1.31x. Moving the discount rate by just 2 points changes the estimate a lot, because r − g in the denominator is a small number. Common slip: assuming the rate barely matters gives 1.00x.

questions.prompt: True or false? Amazon.com (AMZN)'s gap between price and the one-line DCF in FY2024 was above 235.0%.
questions.explanation: True. Gap between price and the one-line DCF = share price ÷ DCF value per share − 1 = $220.00 ÷ $50.32 − 1 = 337.2%, which is above 235.0%. The gap between an estimate of value and the price is what investors call the margin of safety. A large gap often means the market is assuming very different growth than the model, so question the assumptions first. Prices are a sample snapshot for teaching; valuations move every day.

The gap between an estimate of value and the price is what investors call the margin of safety. A large gap often means the market is assuming very different growth than the model, so question the assumptions first. Prices are a sample snapshot for teaching; valuations move every day. lessons.title: Cycles: why one DCF can mislead
lessons.intro: Some industries, such as memory chips, commodities and autos, move in **cycles**. When supply is tight, prices and margins soar; when capacity catches up, they collapse, sometimes into losses. A DCF built on a peak year multiplies that peak into the far future, so it can overstate value many times over. Built on a trough year, it can understate it. The fix is to look at the full history and use a **normalized**, cycle-average cash flow. This lesson uses real 5-10 year histories to measure how big the swings are.

questions.prompt: Micron Technology (MU)'s free cash flow peaked at $8.5B in FY2018; its average from FY2016 to FY2025 was $1.4B. A DCF built on the peak year would start from how many times the cycle-average FCF?
questions.explanation: Peak FCF vs. average FCF = peak-year FCF ÷ average FCF across the cycle = $8.5B (FY2018) ÷ $1.4B average over FY2016–FY2025 = 6.08x. Because a DCF value is proportional to its starting cash flow, starting from a peak year would inflate the estimate by the same multiple. For a business this cyclical, a cycle-average (normalized) cash flow is a sturdier starting point. Common slip: dividing the wrong way round gives 0.16x.

questions.prompt: Procter & Gamble (PG)'s free cash flow peaked at $16.5B in FY2024; its average from FY2020 to FY2024 was $14.8B. A DCF built on the peak year would start from how many times the cycle-average FCF? Answer as a multiple (e.g. 18.2x).
questions.explanation: Peak FCF vs. average FCF = peak-year FCF ÷ average FCF across the cycle = $16.5B (FY2024) ÷ $14.8B average over FY2020–FY2024 = 1.12x. Because a DCF value is proportional to its starting cash flow, starting from a peak year would inflate the estimate by the same multiple. Here the peak is close to the average, a sign of steadier cash flows; for cyclical companies the gap can be several times.

questions.prompt: Between FY2016 and FY2025, Micron Technology (MU)'s gross margin peaked at 58.9% and bottomed at -9.1%. How wide was the swing, in percentage points?
questions.explanation: Gross-margin swing = highest gross margin − lowest gross margin = 58.9% − (-9.1%) = 68.0% (percentage points). A swing that wide is the signature of a cyclical business: when supply and demand flip, prices and margins move together. Common slip: reporting the average gives 33.3%.

questions.prompt: Between FY2021 and FY2025, Costco Wholesale (COST)'s gross margin peaked at 12.9% and bottomed at 12.1%. How wide was the swing, in percentage points? Answer as a percentage (e.g. 12.5%).
questions.explanation: Gross-margin swing = highest gross margin − lowest gross margin = 12.9% − 12.1% = 0.7% (percentage points). That is a fairly steady range; cyclical businesses such as memory chipmakers can swing by 30 points or more.

questions.prompt: True or false? JPMorgan Chase (JPM) reported a net loss in at least one year between FY2020 and FY2024.
questions.explanation: False: net income was positive every year from FY2020 to FY2024. Consistent profits across the period suggest steadier earnings, though past years don't promise future ones.

questions.explanation: Gross-margin swing = highest gross margin − lowest gross margin. NVIDIA (NVDA), FY2021–FY2025: 75.0% − 56.9% = 18.1% (percentage points). Microsoft (MSFT), FY2021–FY2025: 69.8% − 68.4% = 1.4% (percentage points). So NVIDIA (NVDA) is higher.

questions.explanation: Gross-margin swing = highest gross margin − lowest gross margin. Highest to lowest: NVIDIA (NVDA) 18.1%; Apple (AAPL) 8.7%; Procter & Gamble (PG) 4.0%; Costco Wholesale (COST) 0.7%. (Latest fiscal years differ, so the periods don't line up exactly.)

lessons.title: Your holding's margins
lessons.intro: This lesson uses **your own largest holding**. Everything here is explanation, not a judgment of the investment. You'll work out its gross margin and net margin from the reported numbers, then read the **margin stack**: gross margin at the top, operating margin after running costs, net margin after interest and taxes. Seeing where each cent of a sales dollar goes is the fastest way to understand what kind of business you actually own. Until you link an account, we'll show an example company.

questions.prompt: Your largest holding is {holding.name} ({holding.ticker}). In FY{holding.fy} it had revenue of {holding.revenue} and gross profit of {holding.gross_profit}. What was its gross margin? Answer as a percentage.
questions.explanation: Gross margin = gross profit ÷ revenue = {holding.gross_profit} ÷ {holding.revenue} = {holding.gross_margin}. Out of every $1 of sales, {holding.ticker} kept that share after paying for what it sold.

example.prompt: Your largest holding is Tesla (TSLA). In FY2024 it had revenue of $97.7B and gross profit of $17.4B. What was its gross margin? Answer as a percentage.
example.explanation: Gross margin = gross profit ÷ revenue = $17.4B ÷ $97.7B = 17.9%. Out of every $1 of sales, TSLA kept that share after paying for what it sold.

questions.prompt: {holding.ticker}'s gross margin was {holding.gross_margin}. What does that number measure?
choices: The share of each sales dollar left after every cost, interest and tax
The share of each sales dollar left after paying for the goods or services sold
How much the share price changed over the year
The share of profit paid out as dividends
questions.explanation: Gross margin looks only at the first layer of costs, the cost of revenue. Net margin is the one that includes every cost, interest and tax.

example.prompt: TSLA's gross margin was 17.9%. What does that number measure?
example.explanation: Gross margin looks only at the first layer of costs, the cost of revenue. Net margin is the one that includes every cost, interest and tax.

questions.prompt: {holding.ticker} earned net income of {holding.net_income} on revenue of {holding.revenue} in FY{holding.fy}. What was its net margin? Answer as a percentage.
questions.explanation: Net margin = net income ÷ revenue = {holding.net_income} ÷ {holding.revenue} = {holding.net_margin}. It's the bottom line as a share of sales.

example.prompt: TSLA earned net income of $7.1B on revenue of $97.7B in FY2024. What was its net margin? Answer as a percentage.
example.explanation: Net margin = net income ÷ revenue = $7.1B ÷ $97.7B = 7.3%. It's the bottom line as a share of sales.

questions.prompt: True or false? {holding.ticker}'s operating margin ({holding.operating_margin}) was lower than its gross margin ({holding.gross_margin}).
questions.explanation: Operating margin = gross margin minus operating expenses (R&D, sales, admin) as a share of revenue: {holding.gross_margin} at the gross level vs. {holding.operating_margin} at the operating level.

example.prompt: True or false? TSLA's operating margin (7.2%) was lower than its gross margin (17.9%).
example.explanation: Operating margin = gross margin minus operating expenses (R&D, sales, admin) as a share of revenue: 17.9% at the gross level vs. 7.2% at the operating level.

questions.prompt: The gap between {holding.ticker}'s gross margin ({holding.gross_margin}) and its operating margin ({holding.operating_margin}) mostly reflects what?
choices: Operating expenses such as R&D, sales and administration
questions.explanation: Interest and taxes come after operating income, so they sit between operating margin and net margin, not between gross and operating margin.

example.prompt: The gap between TSLA's gross margin (17.9%) and its operating margin (7.2%) mostly reflects what?
example.explanation: Interest and taxes come after operating income, so they sit between operating margin and net margin, not between gross and operating margin.

lessons.title: Your holding's cash
lessons.intro: Profit is an accounting number; cash is what actually lands in the bank. In this lesson you'll compute **free cash flow** for a company you own (operating cash flow minus capital expenditures), express it as a share of revenue, and check whether its cash covers its debt. These are the same checks from Units 4 and 5, applied to your own holding. Nothing here is a signal to act. It's a way to understand the business behind the ticker. questions.prompt: In FY{holding.fy}, {holding.ticker} generated {holding.operating_cash_flow} of operating cash flow and spent {holding.capex} on capital expenditures. What was its free cash flow? Answer in dollars.

lessons.title: Your holding's valuation
lessons.intro: Now bring in the share price for a company you own. You'll compute its **P/E**, flip it into an **earnings yield**, reverse-engineer the **growth the price implies**, and compare its **FCF yield** with its dividend yield. None of this says whether the price is right. Valuation numbers describe what the market is currently assuming, and they change every day. Treat them as questions to investigate, not answers. Until you link an account, we'll show an example company.

questions.prompt: {holding.ticker}'s share price was {holding.price} and its FY{holding.fy} diluted EPS was {holding.eps_diluted}. What was its P/E ratio? Answer as a multiple.
questions.explanation: P/E = price ÷ EPS = {holding.price} ÷ {holding.eps_diluted} = {holding.pe}. The market was paying that many dollars per $1 of last year's earnings. Prices are sample snapshots and change daily.

example.prompt: AMZN's share price was $220.00 and its FY2024 diluted EPS was $5.53. What was its P/E ratio? Answer as a multiple.
example.explanation: P/E = price ÷ EPS = $220.00 ÷ $5.53 = 39.8x. The market was paying that many dollars per $1 of last year's earnings. Prices are sample snapshots and change daily.

questions.prompt: {holding.ticker} traded at a P/E of {holding.pe}, an earnings yield of {holding.earnings_yield}. Which statement is accurate?
choices: A higher P/E means the company earned more profit
Earnings yield is 1 ÷ P/E, so a higher P/E means a lower earnings yield
P/E and earnings yield are unrelated numbers
Earnings yield is the dividend the company pays each year
questions.explanation: Earnings yield = EPS ÷ price = 1 ÷ P/E. At {holding.pe}, that's {holding.earnings_yield}.

example.prompt: AMZN traded at a P/E of 39.8x, an earnings yield of 2.5%. Which statement is accurate?
example.explanation: Earnings yield = EPS ÷ price = 1 ÷ P/E. At 39.8x, that's 2.5%.

questions.prompt: Using return ≈ earnings yield + growth and a 9% required return, what long-run growth rate does {holding.ticker}'s P/E of {holding.pe} imply? Answer as a percentage.
questions.explanation: Implied growth ≈ 9% − earnings yield = 9% − {holding.earnings_yield} = {holding.implied_growth}. This is what the current price already assumes, not a forecast.

example.prompt: Using return ≈ earnings yield + growth and a 9% required return, what long-run growth rate does AMZN's P/E of 39.8x imply? Answer as a percentage.
example.explanation: Implied growth ≈ 9% − earnings yield = 9% − 2.5% = 6.5%. This is what the current price already assumes, not a forecast.

questions.prompt: {holding.ticker} produced {holding.free_cash_flow} of free cash flow and had a market cap of {holding.market_cap}. What was its FCF yield? Answer as a percentage.
questions.explanation: FCF yield = free cash flow ÷ market cap = {holding.free_cash_flow} ÷ {holding.market_cap} = {holding.fcf_yield}.

example.prompt: AMZN produced $32.9B of free cash flow and had a market cap of $2.36T. What was its FCF yield? Answer as a percentage.
example.explanation: FCF yield = free cash flow ÷ market cap = $32.9B ÷ $2.36T = 1.4%.

questions.prompt: True or false? {holding.ticker}'s FCF yield ({holding.fcf_yield}) was higher than its dividend yield ({holding.dividend_yield}).
questions.explanation: If FCF yield exceeds dividend yield, the dividend was covered by free cash flow with room to spare; the rest can go to buybacks, debt paydown or reinvestment.
